criteria.descriptor: Correctly describes watermark/cursor incremental extraction on `updated_at`, an idempotent upsert/merge keyed on the primary key, commit-then-checkpoint ordering, and backoff on 429. No false claims (e.g. that append avoids duplicates, that `updated_since` returns deletes, or that timestamps are perfectly unique/monotonic).

Addresses all three required parts — incremental extraction, the sink guarantee against duplicates and lost updates, and at least two concrete failure/edge cases (deletes, rate limits/pagination, crash recovery, or schema evolution) — rather than only one or two.

Justifies choices by mechanism: why `updated_at` over `created_at`, why an overlap window is needed, why upsert makes at-least-once extraction safe, and why the checkpoint must follow the durable commit — not just a list of steps.

Presents a structured, reviewable design using precise vocabulary (watermark/cursor, idempotent merge, at-least-once vs exactly-once, tombstone/reconciliation) that a reviewer could implement from directly.

expected_answer_points: Uses an incremental high-watermark/cursor on `updated_at` (last-modified), not `created_at`, so updated records re-enter the delta, and persists that cursor across runs

Applies an overlap/lookback safety margin (and `>=`) to tolerate clock skew, late-committing transactions, and same-timestamp boundaries — deliberately accepting at-least-once extraction rather than risking missed rows
Writes to the target with an idempotent UPSERT/MERGE keyed on the primary key (not append/INSERT), so retries and overlapping re-pulls stay duplicate-free — effectively exactly-once in the sink
Advances/persists the watermark checkpoint only after the batch durably commits, so a mid-run crash resumes without gaps and never advances on a partial pull
Handles pagination completely and rate limits (429 → exponential backoff with jitter, honor Retry-After), and does not advance the watermark on an incomplete run
Recognizes that incremental `updated_since` cannot surface hard deletes, and proposes soft-delete/tombstone handling or periodic reconciliation/full refresh to prune them
Lands raw payloads in staging and tolerates schema evolution (store raw JSON / additive fields) to keep ingestion replayable
common_pitfalls: Uses `created_at` instead of `updated_at` as the cursor, so status changes to existing orders never re-enter the delta and are silently missed
Appends/INSERTs rows instead of UPSERT/MERGE on `id`, producing duplicates whenever a record is updated or a batch is retried
Advances the watermark before the load durably commits, so a crash between pull and commit permanently loses records (or double-advances and skips a range)
Uses strict `>` on an exact watermark with no overlap/lookback, assuming timestamps are unique and monotonic — missing rows that share the boundary second or commit late under clock skew
Assumes the incremental `updated_since` delta will capture deletes, so hard-deleted orders linger in the warehouse forever
Conflates at-least-once delivery with duplicated rows in the sink, not realizing an idempotent upsert makes retries and overlap re-pulls harmless
reference_answer:
Replace the full reload with a watermark-based incremental pull.

Extraction (incremental): Keep a high-watermark cursor on the record's last-modified timestamp `updated_at`, NOT `created_at` — status changes must re-enter the delta, and created_at never moves. Persist the watermark after each successful run. Each run calls `GET /orders?updated_since=<watermark>` and pages through every page until exhausted. Because vendor clocks, commit ordering, and same-second boundaries are unreliable, subtract a small safety lookback (e.g. a few minutes) from the stored watermark and query with `>=`; this deliberately over-fetches a small overlap rather than risking gaps. Extraction is therefore at-least-once by design.

Correctness in the sink (no duplicates, no lost updates): Land raw payloads in a staging/bronze table, then MERGE/UPSERT into the target keyed on the primary key `id`, taking the row with the newest `updated_at`. Upsert — not INSERT/append — is what makes the pipeline idempotent: re-processing the overlap window or replaying a failed batch overwrites the same row instead of duplicating it, so at-least-once extraction becomes effectively exactly-once in the table.

Checkpointing: Advance the persisted watermark only after the batch is durably committed (same transaction or atomic swap). A mid-run crash then restarts from the old watermark and re-pulls harmlessly, because the load is idempotent. Never advance on a partial or failed pull.

Edge cases:
- Rate limits / pagination: on HTTP 429 back off exponentially with jitter and honor `Retry-After`; if not all pages were retrieved, treat the run as failed and do not advance the watermark.
- Deletes: `updated_since` never returns hard-deleted rows, so they would linger forever. Use the API's soft-delete/tombstone flag if present, or run a periodic full reconciliation (anti-join current IDs against the source) to prune.
- Schema evolution: store the raw JSON payload so new/optional fields don't break ingestion; project columns downstream.

Watermark cursor + idempotent upsert + commit-then-checkpoint together give incremental, resumable, exactly-once-into-warehouse ingestion.
